title: Binary search trees: search, traversal, insert and delete
summary: Why ordered data needs more than a hash table; the tree vocabulary and the BST property; search, min, max and successor; in-, pre- and post-order traversal; insert as a new leaf; the three delete cases (leaf, one child, two children with the successor); and why every operation is O(h), which is O(log n) balanced and O(n) when keys arrive sorted.
sourceNote: Lecture 12 'Binary Search Trees' (Wed Sep 30) slides and HW 12, CLRS 10.4 and 12.1 to 12.3. The example tree (15 at the root), insert 10, the deletes of 5, 7 and 3, the traversal orders, the product-price tree and the applications are Poon's. HW 12 answers are computed by the script that builds this chapter.

sections.heading: The big picture: fast AND in order

blocks.md: Last lecture's hash table does search, insert and delete in O(1). But it scatters keys on purpose, so it has **no order**. Ask it 'which products cost between $20 and $50?' or 'what's the cheapest?' and it has to look at every single item: O(n). A sorted array is great at order but slow to change. A **binary search tree** gets most of both.

blocks.title: Poon's performance table, plus the BST row (h = the tree's height)

data.question: Keep data sorted AND cheap to change

blocks.md: **Why it matters** Every 'sorted map' you'll use (Java's `TreeMap`, a database index answering `WHERE age > 25`) is a balanced BST underneath. The midterm traces insert and delete on a tree by hand, and next lecture (AVL trees) only makes sense once this one does.
blocks.label: why

sections.heading: Tree words, one at a time

blocks.body: A set of **nodes** connected by edges in a hierarchy. Each node can have zero or more children, and every node except the top one has **exactly one parent**. Unlike an array or list, it isn't a line: it branches.
One item in the tree: a **key**, often a **value**, and pointers to its children.
The **root** is the top-most node. A node is the **parent** of the nodes it points to, its **children**. A **leaf** has no children.
A node and everything below it. It is a tree on its own, with its own root.
A node's **depth** is the number of edges from the root down to it (the root has depth 0). The tree's **height** is the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf.

blocks.body: A tree where every node has **at most two** children, called the **left child** and the **right child**.

blocks.prompt: In Poon's example tree, what is the depth of 13, and is it a leaf?
blocks.answer: Depth **3** (15 → 6 → 7 → 13). Not a leaf: it has a left child, 9.

blocks.prompt: What is the height of a tree with only a root?
blocks.answer: **0**: the longest root-to-leaf path has no edges. (An empty tree is usually given height −1.)

sections.heading: The BST property: the one rule

blocks.body: For **every** node x: every key in x's **left subtree** is **less** than x.key, and every key in x's **right subtree** is **greater**. A tree where this holds at every node is a **binary search tree**.

blocks.caption: The rule at node 6: the whole left subtree (2, 3, 5) is smaller, the whole right subtree (7, 9, 13) is bigger. Hover the nodes.

blocks.body: The rule is about whole **subtrees**, not just children. A tree where every left child is smaller than its parent and every right child bigger can still break the BST property: put 16 as the right child of 13 in the example, and 16 is bigger than 13 but sits in 15's LEFT subtree, where everything must be smaller than 15.

blocks.md: **Duplicates.** Most BST implementations simply ignore an insert of a key that's already there (Poon's slide). When many items share a key, the node stores a list instead, like his product example below.

blocks.title: Poon's product example
blocks.body:
Key = price. Each node keeps the list of products at that price.

          $50 [Chair]
         /          \
   $20 [Book]      $80 [Desk]
    /      \             \
$10 [...]  $35 [Lamp]    $90 [Monitor, headphones]

class BSTNode {
  double price;             // the key
  List<Product> products;   // the value
  BSTNode left, right;
}

'Everything from $20 to $50' = walk just the part of the tree between those keys.

blocks.prompt: Is this a BST? Root 10, left child 5, right child 12, and 5's right child is 11.
blocks.answer: **No.** 11 is in 10's LEFT subtree but 11 > 10. Every key left of 10 must be smaller than 10.

blocks.md: **The search idea.** Compare with the node you're at. Equal: found. Smaller: the key can only be on the left. Bigger: only on the right. Each comparison throws away a whole subtree, exactly like binary search throws away half an array.

frames.caption: search(root, 13). Start at the root and compare. Every step goes down ONE level, left or right.
13 < 15, so everything that could match is in the left subtree. The other side is never looked at.
13 > 6, so everything that could match is in the right subtree. The other side is never looked at.
13 > 7, so everything that could match is in the right subtree. The other side is never looked at.
root.key == 13: found it. Return this node. 4 nodes looked at, one per level.

blocks.title: search(root, 16): a key that isn't there

frames.caption: search(root, 16). Start at the root and compare. Every step goes down ONE level, left or right.
16 > 15, so everything that could match is in the right subtree. The other side is never looked at.
16 < 18, so everything that could match is in the left subtree. The other side is never looked at.
16 < 17, so everything that could match is in the left subtree. The other side is never looked at.
root is None: we fell off the tree. 16 is not in it. Return None.

blocks.title: Min and max: keep going left, keep going right

frames.caption: The minimum: start at the root and keep going LEFT until there is no left child.
At 15: it has a left child (6), keep going.
At 6: it has a left child (3), keep going.
At 3: it has a left child (2), keep going.
At 2: no left child. 2 is the minimum.
The maximum: the same walk to the RIGHT.
Right, right, right: 15 → 18 → 20. The maximum is 20. Both walks follow ONE path: O(h).

blocks.body: The **successor** of a key is the next bigger key in the tree (the smallest key greater than it). The **predecessor** is the next smaller one. In sorted order 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 13, 15, …, the successor of 13 is 15.

rows: The node has a right child
the **minimum of its right subtree**: go right once, then left all the way
walk **up** until you arrive from a LEFT child; that parent is it
No right child and you never arrive from the left
blocks.title: Finding the successor (Poon's two cases)

frames.caption: Successor of 6 = the next key in sorted order (7). Case 1: 6 HAS a right child, so the successor is the minimum of that right subtree.
Go to the right child, 7, then left as far as possible. 7 has no left child, so the successor of 6 is 7.
Successor of 15: right child 18, then left as far as possible: 17. So 17.
Successor of 13. Case 2: 13 has NO right child. Walk UP until you come up from a LEFT child.
13 is the RIGHT child of 7, so keep going up.
7 is the RIGHT child of 6, so keep going up.
6 is the LEFT child of 15. Stop: 15 is the successor of 13 (check the sorted order: … 9, 13, 15, …).
And 20? No right child, and walking up we only ever come from right children, all the way past the root. 20 is the maximum: no successor.

blocks.prompt: In the example tree, what is the successor of 5?
blocks.answer: 5 has no right child, so walk up: 5 is the RIGHT child of 3, keep going; 3 is the LEFT child of 6, stop. Successor = **6**.
The mirror rule: the maximum of the LEFT subtree. Go left to 6, then right as far as possible: 7, 13. Predecessor = **13**.

blocks.body: Visiting every node of the tree exactly once, in some order. The three orders differ only in **when** the node itself is visited compared with its two subtrees.

sections.heading: Insert: a new key becomes a leaf

blocks.body: Walk down exactly like search. When you reach an empty spot, put the new node there. A new key **always becomes a leaf**; nothing already in the tree moves.

blocks.title: insert(root, 10): the slide's example, line by line

frames.caption: insert(root, 10). A new key always becomes a LEAF. Walk down exactly like search, until the spot is empty.
10 < 15: go left.
10 ≥ 6: go right.
10 ≥ 7: go right.
10 < 13: go left.
10 ≥ 9: go right. 9.right is empty, so that's where 10 goes.
root is None: line 3 makes a new Node(10) and returns it. The caller stores it in 9.right.
Every call returns its root, so each parent re-links the same child it had (nothing changes above the new leaf). Still a BST: the in-order is still sorted.

blocks.md: **Why insert returns root.** In Java (and Python), reassigning a parameter inside a function doesn't change the caller's variable. So each call **returns** the root of its subtree, and the caller stores it back: `root.left = insert(root.left, key)`. Where nothing changed, the same child is stored back. At the empty spot, the returned node is the new one, and that's how it gets linked in (Poon's 'node relinking' slide).

blocks.prompt: Insert 16 into the example tree. Where does it go?
blocks.answer: 16 > 15 → right to 18; 16 < 18 → left to 17; 16 < 17 → 17's left is empty. **16 becomes the left child of 17.**

rows: just remove it: the parent's link becomes null
the child takes its place: the parent points straight at the child
copy the **successor's** key into the node, then delete the successor from the right subtree
blocks.title: The three delete cases

frames.caption: delete(root, 5). First find it, the same walk as search: 15 → 6 → 3 → 5.
Found 5 (line 8). It has a leaf.
Case 1, a leaf: root.left is None, so return root.right, which is None. 3's link becomes None and 5 is gone.
delete(root, 7). First find it, the same walk as search: 15 → 6 → 7.
Found 7 (line 8). It has one child (13).
Case 2, one child: return the child, 13. The parent 6 now points straight at 13, and 7's whole subtree moves up one level with it.

blocks.title: delete(root, 3): two children, using the successor

frames.caption: delete(root, 3). First find it, the same walk as search: 15 → 6 → 3.
Found 3 (line 8). It has two children (2, 5).
Case 3, two children. We can't just unlink 3. Find its SUCCESSOR: the minimum of its right subtree. Go right to 5, then left as far as possible: 5.
Copy the successor's key UP into 3's node (line 14). 5 is the smallest key bigger than everything on the left, and smaller than everything else on the right, so it fits exactly where 3 was.
Line 15: delete the old 5 from the right subtree. It has at most one child (it had no left child, or it wouldn't be the minimum), so this is always Case 1 or 2.
Done: 3 is gone, 5 took its place. In-order still sorted: 2, 5, 6, 7, 9, 13, 15, 17, 18, 20.

blocks.md: **Why the successor works.** The successor is the smallest key in the right subtree. That makes it bigger than everything on the left and smaller than everything else on the right: exactly the rule the replaced node had to follow. And it has no left child (it's a minimum), so removing it is always the easy case, never another two-children case.
blocks.label: think

blocks.body: Two slips cost points here. Taking the successor from the LEFT subtree (that's the predecessor; also valid, but not what Poon's code does, so your answer won't match). And forgetting the second step: after copying the successor's key up, the old successor node still has to be deleted, or the key appears twice.

blocks.prompt: HW 12 Question 3a: in the tree from inserting 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7, 13, delete 6.
blocks.answer:
6 has two children (4 and 7). Its successor is the minimum of its right subtree: **7**. Copy 7 up into 6's node, then delete the old 7 (a leaf). The tree:

  level 0: 8
  level 1: 3 (L of 8), 10 (R of 8)
  level 2: 1 (L of 3), 7 (R of 3), 14 (R of 10)
  level 3: 4 (L of 7), 13 (L of 14)

8 is the root with two children. Successor = minimum of the right subtree = **10** (10 has no left child). Copy 10 up, delete the old 10 (it has one child, 14, which moves up). The tree:

  level 0: 10
  level 1: 3 (L of 10), 14 (R of 10)
  level 2: 1 (L of 3), 7 (R of 3), 13 (L of 14)
  level 3: 4 (L of 7)

In-order: 1, 3, 4, 7, 10, 13, 14.

sections.heading: How fast? It depends on the height

blocks.md: **Every operation walks one path.** search, insert, delete, min, max and successor all go from the root down one branch (successor sometimes up one branch). A path is at most as long as the tree is tall, so each is **O(h)**.

blocks.title: Performance depends on the insertion order (Poon's slide)
Sorted insertions build a linked list

frames.caption: insert(1): the first key is the root.
insert(2): bigger than everything so far, so it goes right, right, right… Height is now 1.
insert(3): bigger than everything so far, so it goes right, right, right… Height is now 2.
insert(4): bigger than everything so far, so it goes right, right, right… Height is now 3.
insert(5): bigger than everything so far, so it goes right, right, right… Height is now 4.
insert(6): bigger than everything so far, so it goes right, right, right… Height is now 5.
insert(7): bigger than everything so far, so it goes right, right, right… Height is now 6.
7 keys inserted in sorted order give a tree of height 6 = n − 1. It's a linked list wearing a tree costume: search is O(n).

blocks.prompt: HW 12 Question 4: give 7 insertions into an empty BST that produce the maximum possible height. What is the height, and what does search cost?
blocks.answer: Insert them **in sorted order**, e.g. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 (reverse order works too). Every key goes right, so the tree is a chain: height **6** (n − 1 edges). Search may walk the whole chain: **O(n)**.

blocks.md: **Next lecture: AVL trees.** A plain BST can't stop you from inserting sorted data. An AVL tree rebalances itself after every insert and delete, so its height stays O(log n) no matter what order the keys come in.

cards.title: Sorted maps and sets
lines: Keys come back in order; floor/ceiling queries are O(log n).

cards.title: Database indexes
lines: A hash index can't answer that without a full scan; an ordered index walks just the matching part.

cards.title: Memory and file systems
lines: Track allocated blocks sorted by address.
Finding a free block or merging neighbours is a quick ordered lookup.

blocks.md: **Where you've already met this.** In an app, 'show my assignments due between Monday and Friday, earliest first' is a range query over dates. With the data in a hash map, you'd sort everything every time; with an ordered index (a balanced BST or its cousin, the B-tree), you walk just that week.
